exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with polyuria and RPG 12.5 mmol/L. What is your next step? — Confirm diabetes diagnosis; arrange HbA1c and start metformin if no contraindications.

A patient with known type 1 diabetes arrives unconscious, RPG 30 mmol/L, ketones positive. What immediate management is required? — Initiate IV fluids, insulin infusion, and correct electrolytes; monitor glucose hourly.
How does severe dehydration affect a random glucose result? — It can falsely raise the value, so assess clinical volume status and repeat after rehydration if needed.
Which drug class should be avoided in a patient with renal failure presenting with high RPG? — Sulfonylureas, because they increase hypoglycaemia risk when clearance is reduced.

What distinguishes diabetic ketoacidosis from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state on investigation? — DKA shows metabolic acidosis and positive ketones; HHS shows very high glucose (>33 mmol/L) without significant ketosis.

In a low‑resource clinic without HbA1c, how can you monitor long‑term control? — Use serial random or fasting glucose measurements and urine dipstick for glucosuria, combined with clinical assessment.
Why might a patient on rifampicin have an elevated RPG? — Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, increasing insulin resistance and precipitating secondary diabetes.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for a patient with newly diagnosed diabetes? — Persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, or altered mental status suggesting DKA/HHS.
ai.title: Random Plasma Glucose
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Random plasma glucose (RPG) measures blood sugar at any time, useful for diagnosing diabetes when symptoms are present. In low‑resource settings it guides urgent treatment and further testing.

b: ≥11.1 mmol/L with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, or blurred vision = diabetes
Used when fasting or OGTT not feasible
sections.p: RPG is the concentration of glucose in plasma drawn at any time, without fasting. In a symptomatic patient a value ≥11.1 mmol/L confirms diabetes mellitus.

b: New diagnosis: first RPG ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms
Uncontrolled: RPG often >13.9 mmol/L, HbA1c ≥9 % (75 mmol/mol)
sections.p: Diabetes is staged by chronic complications rather than a single glucose cut‑off. RPG helps identify new‑onset disease; subsequent HbA1c and fasting glucose define control.

b: Type 2 diabetes (obesity, sedentary lifestyle)
Type 1 diabetes (autoimmune, often in children)
Gestational diabetes (pregnancy)
Secondary diabetes from HIV antiretrovirals, TB treatment (rifampicin), chronic pancreatitis, or steroid use

b: Polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss
Fatigue, blurred vision, recurrent infections
In severe hyperglycaemia: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, altered mental status
sections.p: Patients present with classic hyperglycaemic symptoms or as incidental findings during acute illness.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical picture and repeat RPG later; use urine dipstick as a surrogate for glucose and ketones.

t.b: Does the patient meet diagnostic criteria for diabetes? ≥11.1 mmol/L with symptoms confirms diabetes.
What is chronic glycaemic control? ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5 %) confirms diabetes; higher values indicate poor control.

t.a: Fasting plasma glucose (if patient can fast)
t.b: Is the hyperglycaemia persistent? ≥7.0 mmol/L confirms diabetes.

t.a: Urine dipstick for glucose and ketones
t.b: Is there glucosuria or ketoacidosis? Positive ketones suggest diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

t.a: Serum electrolytes, creatinine, and venous blood gas (if DKA suspected)
t.b: Are there metabolic derangements requiring urgent treatment? Look for acidosis, hyperkalaemia, renal impairment.

b: Diabetic ketoacidosis: vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, altered consciousness
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: RPG >33 mmol/L, dehydration, seizures
Infections (UTI, skin, TB) that worsen hyperglycaemia
Rapid progression to retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
sections.p: Unrecognised or poorly controlled diabetes leads to acute and chronic threats.

b: If DKA/HHS suspected: start IV fluids, insulin infusion, correct electrolytes; monitor glucose hourly
For newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes without emergency: start metformin (first‑line) unless contraindicated (renal failure, pregnancy)
Avoid sulfonylureas in patients with renal impairment or at risk of hypoglycaemia
Educate on diet, exercise, and self‑monitoring; arrange follow‑up for HbA1c
sections.p: Treat the underlying diabetes and address any acute metabolic emergency.

b: Check HbA1c every 3 months (or 6 months if stable)
Screen for retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy annually
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and influenza
Promote lifestyle modification: weight control, physical activity, reduced sugary foods
sections.p: Long‑term care aims to keep glucose within target and prevent complications.

b: Stress‑induced hyperglycaemia (acute illness, surgery)
Cushing’s syndrome (chronic cortisol excess)
Pancreatic endocrine tumours (insulinoma causes low glucose, not high)
sections.p: Conditions that can cause high glucose but are not diabetes.

b: Recent food intake may raise glucose without diabetes
Severe dehydration can falsely elevate glucose
Laboratory error: haemolysis or delayed processing

whenToSeekHelp: Altered consciousness, seizures, or rapid breathing (possible DKA/HHS)
Persistent vomiting with inability to keep fluids down
Signs of severe dehydration (dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, low blood pressure)
